title: Zheng He's Treasure Voyages
intro: The Yongle Emperor ordered the construction of a treasure fleet in 1403, and Admiral Zheng He was commissioned to command it. It made seven voyages to the South China Sea and the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433, six under the Yongle Emperor and the seventh under the Xuande Emperor.
ending: The seventh voyage returned in 1433 with envoys from 11 countries, including one from Mecca. It is not exactly known why the voyages ended.

stops.text: The fleet assembled at Nanjing in the autumn of 1405 and made ready to depart. The Yongle Emperor had held a banquet for the crew the evening before the maiden voyage.
stops.quote: In the autumn of 1405, the fleet had assembled at Nanjing and was ready to depart from the city.

stops.text: After waiting at Changle for the northeast monsoon, the fleet left the Fujian coast. Champa was the first foreign destination, and the port of Qui Nhon was always the first the fleet visited.
stops.quote: The port of Qui Nhon in Champa was always the first foreign destination that the fleet visited.

stops.text: The fleet called at Malacca on the way out and stopped there again on its return journey to China.
stops.quote: During the return, the fleet stopped at Malacca again.

stops.text: On the Malabar Coast, the fleet went as far as Calicut. Mills states that it may have stayed four months there, from December to April 1407.
stops.quote: Mills (1970) states that the fleet may have stayed four months at Calicut from December to April 1407.

stops.text: On the return trip Zheng and his associates fought the pirate fleet of Chen Zuyi, who had seized Palembang and dominated the route through the Strait of Malacca. Chen's fleet was defeated.
stops.quote: During the return trip in 1407, Zheng and his associates engaged Chen Zuyi and his pirate fleet in battle at Palembang.

stops.text: The fleet returned to Nanjing. Foreign envoys from Calicut, Quilon, Semudera, Aru, Malacca and other nations had come with it to present tribute at the Ming court.
stops.quote: The fleet returned to Nanjing on 2 October 1407.

stops.text: The fleet settled the enmity between Ming China and Java. In a civil war a King of West Java had killed 170 members of a Chinese embassy, and the Ming court demanded 60,000 liang of gold in compensation.
stops.quote: In this voyage, the Chinese forcibly settled the enmity between Ming China and Java.

stops.text: The fleet was tasked with the formal investiture of Mana Vikraan as King of Calicut. A tablet was placed in Calicut to commemorate the relationship between China and India.
stops.quote: The fleet was tasked to carry out the formal investiture of Mana Vikraan as the King of Calicut.

stops.text: On the outward journey the fleet landed at Galle in Ceylon. There Zheng set up a trilingual inscription in Chinese, Tamil and Persian, praising the Buddha, the local god Tenavarai Nayanar and Allah.
stops.quote: The fleet landed at Galle, Ceylon, in 1410.

stops.text: On the homeward journey Zheng and 2,000 troops went overland into Kotte, where King Alakeshvara had lured them. The Chinese invaded Kotte, captured its capital and took Alakeshvara and his family captive.
stops.quote: In response, Zheng and his troops invaded Kotte and captured its capital.

stops.text: The fleet sailed beyond Calicut for the first time, through the Maldive and Laccadive Islands to Hormuz.
stops.quote: They proceeded to Liushan (Maldive and Laccadive Islands), Bila (Bitra Atoll), Sunla (Chetlat Atoll), and Hormuz.

stops.text: On the way home the fleet stopped in northern Sumatra, where Zheng was ordered to attack the usurper Sekandar. The Ming forces defeated him and pursued his forces to Lambri, where they captured him, his wife and his child.
stops.quote: In 1415, the fleet made a stop at northern Sumatra during the journey homeward. In this region, Sekandar had usurped the Semudera throne from Zain al-'Abidin

stops.text: Zheng may have left the Chinese coast in the autumn of 1417, first making port at Quanzhou to load porcelain and other goods. A Ming tablet there records him burning incense for divine protection for the voyage.
stops.quote: A Ming tablet at Quanzhou commemorates Zheng burning incense for divine protection for the voyage on 31 May 1417.

stops.text: A Yemeni chronicle reports that Chinese ships reached the Aden coast in January 1419, and that they did not leave the Rasulid capital at Ta'izz before 19 March.
stops.quote: The Tarih al-Yaman fi d-daulati r-Rasuliya reports that Chinese ships reached the Aden coast in January 1419 and did not leave the Rasulid capital at Ta'izz before 19 March.

stops.text: Mogadishu lay on the most likely route for Arabia and East Africa, which ran by Hormuz, Lasa, Aden, Mogadishu, Brava, Zhubu and Malindi. The fleet returned to China on 8 August 1419.
stops.quote: For Arabia and East Africa, the most likely route was Hormuz, Lasa, Aden, Mogadishu, Brava, Zhubu, and then Malindi.

stops.text: The fleet probably called at Brava after Mogadishu on this voyage. Contemporary Chinese porcelain has been excavated at the East African places the fleet visited.
stops.quote: For Arabia and East Africa, the most likely route was Hormuz, Lasa, Aden, Mogadishu, Brava, Zhubu, and then Malindi.

stops.text: Malindi was probably the last place on the route for the fifth voyage, and the farthest south on the East African coast among its stops.
stops.quote: For Arabia and East Africa, the most likely route was Hormuz, Lasa, Aden, Mogadishu, Brava, Zhubu, and then Malindi.

stops.text: After the fleet divided at Semudera, detached squadrons went on to destinations including the three Arabian states of Dhofar, Lasa and Aden.
stops.quote: The squadrons traveled from there to their respective destinations at Liushan (Maldive and Laccadive Islands), Hormuz at the Persian Gulf, the three Arabian states of Dhofar, Lasa, and Aden, and the two African states of Mogadishu and Brava.

stops.text: The eunuch Zhou, probably Zhou Man, led a detached squadron to Aden. The fleet returned to China on 3 September 1422 with envoys from Siam, Semudera, Aden and other countries.
stops.quote: The eunuch Zhou (probably Zhou Man) led a detached squadron to Aden.

stops.text: After leaving Nanjing on 19 January 1431, the fleet reached Surabaya in Java and departed on 13 July, according to the Xia Xiyang.
stops.quote: They arrived at Surabaya in Java on 7 March and departed from there on 13 July.

stops.text: Fei Xin writes that the fleet anchored for three days at Cuilanxu, probably Great Nicobar Island, because of unfavourable winds and waves. Local men and women came in log boats to trade coconuts.
stops.quote: He writes that, on 14 November 1432, the fleet arrived at Cuilanxu (probably the Great Nicobar Island) where it anchored for three days due to the unfavorable winds and waves.

stops.text: The fleet arrived at Calicut on 10 December and left four days later, on 14 December.
stops.quote: They arrived at Calicut on 10 December and departed from there on 14 December.

stops.text: The fleet arrived at Hormuz, the farthest west of the eight destinations the Xia Xiyang records for this voyage, and left on 9 March.
stops.quote: They arrived at Hormuz on 17 January 1433 and departed from there on 9 March.

stops.text: Ma Huan writes that Hong sent seven men from Calicut with a ship bound for Mecca. They took a year to go and return, and bought giraffes, lions and ostriches.
stops.quote: Ma writes that Hong sent seven men to accompany a ship from Calicut bound for Mecca after he observed that Calicut was sending men there.

stops.text: On the return the fleet arrived at Taicang. The Xia Xiyang did not record the later stages of the journey to the capital.
stops.quote: The fleet arrived at Taicang on 7 July.

stops.text: The fleet arrived at the capital, Beijing. On 27 July the Xuande Emperor bestowed ceremonial robes and paper money on its personnel.
stops.quote: On 22 July 1433, they arrived in the capital Beijing.

notes: Dates marked as ranges or inferred: Calicut first voyage ('December to April 1407', Mills, 'may have'); Java and Calicut on the second voyage (departure 'late 1407 or possibly early 1408', the quotes do not carry the year); Hormuz on the fourth voyage (no date given for the visit; year 1414 is only the voyage midpoint); Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi (the article gives a 'most likely route', no dates; I give 1419 because the fleet returned 8 August 1419); sixth-voyage Dhofar and Aden (voyage years only); Mecca (Ma Huan's account, year inferred from the voyage's end). Seventh-voyage Calicut: article gives day and month, 1432 inferred from the entries before and after. Entry for Champa is the kingdom's entry, the stop is its port Qui Nhon. Ta'izz (entry taiz) is in the Aden quote, not given its own stop. Left out: Liujiagang, Changle (no sure Wikipedia title), Lambri, Pulau Sembilan, Siam, Cochin, Quilon, Colombo, Bengal, Zhubu, Lasa. The article is unsure whether Zheng sailed on the second voyage and whether he went in person to the Arabian and African places; detached squadrons did much of it.
